title: They that be wise shall shine (Daniel 12:3)
hookLine: the wise "shall shine as the brightness of the firmament"

cards: What does a book of furnaces and lions end on? Not on a court story.

The later chapters of Daniel turn into visions: beasts rising from the sea, kings rising and falling, messengers who explain and still leave much unexplained. By the last chapter the vision has reached its darkest point.

In the King James words, "there shall be a time of trouble, such as never was since there was a nation even to that same time." And right there, in the trouble, the text stops to say who will be shining.

teach.b: Here's the line: "And they that be wise shall shine as the brightness of the firmament; and they that turn many to righteousness as the stars for ever and ever." Two kinds of light.
The firmament is the whole sky, the bright dome over everything. The stars are points of light, each on its own in the dark. Who are the wise?
The Hebrew word is maskilim. A chapter earlier, the same book describes them: "they that understand among the people shall instruct many."

teach.h: THE WISE ARE THE ONES WHO INSTRUCT.
teach.b: So in Daniel, the wise aren't the ones who keep wisdom to themselves. They pass it on, and those who turn many to righteousness shine like stars.
Some readers hear in maskilim both at once: those who are wise, and those who make others wise. Then a surprise near the very end.

teach.h: I HEARD, BUT I UNDERSTOOD NOT.
teach.b: Daniel himself, who read the wall and the dreams of kings, says of his own vision: "I heard, but I understood not."

teach.h: THEY THAT BE WISE SHALL SHINE.
teach.b: He asks how it will end, and is told: "Go thy way, Daniel: for the words are closed up and sealed till the time of the end." The man who read the wall doesn't get every answer, and he's still told to go his way.
You don't need to understand everything to teach the one thing you do.
A star doesn't light the whole sky. It shines where it is.

how: In chavruta, a traditional way of Jewish study in pairs, two partners read a text aloud and explain it to each other, so that teaching is part of learning.

Think of one person who might like to hear it, and say the sentence to yourself, plainly, the way you'd say it to them; one star's worth is enough.
